In [[differential geometry]], a '''quaternion-Kähler manifold''' (or '''quaternionic Kähler manifold''') is a Riemannian 4''n''-manifold whose [[holonomy|Riemannian holonomy group]] is a subgroup of Sp(''n'')·Sp(1) for some <math>n\geq 2</math>. Here Sp(''n'') is the sub-group of <math>SO(4n)</math> consisting of those orthogonal transformations that arise by '''left'''-multiplication by some quaternionic <math>n \times n </math> matrix, while the group <math>Sp(1) = S^3</math> of unit-length quaternions instead acts on quaternionic <math>n</math>-space <math>{\mathbb H}^n = {\mathbb R}^{4n}</math> by '''right''' scalar multiplication. The [[Lie group]] <math>Sp(n)\cdot Sp(1) \subset SO(4n)</math> generated by combining these actions is then abstractly isomorphic to <math>[Sp(n) \times Sp(1) ]/{\mathbb Z}_2</math>.

Although the above loose version of the definition includes [[hyperkähler manifold]]s, the standard convention of excluding these will be followed by also requiring that the [[scalar curvature]] be non-zero&mdash; as is automatically true if the holonomy group equals the entire group Sp(''n'')·Sp(1).

== Early history ==

[[Marcel Berger]]'s 1955 paper<ref>{{cite journal |first=Marcel |last=Berger |title=Sur les groups d'holonomie des variétés à connexion affine et des variétés riemanniennes |journal=Bull. Soc. Math. France |volume=83 |pages=279–330 |year=1955 |doi=10.24033/bsmf.1464 |url=http://www.numdam.org/article/BSMF_1955__83__279_0.pdf |doi-access=free }}</ref> on the classification of Riemannian holonomy groups first raised the issue of the existence of non-symmetric manifolds with holonomy Sp(''n'')·Sp(1). Interesting results were proved in the mid-1960s in pioneering work by [[Edmond Bonan]]<ref>{{cite journal |first=Edmond |last=Bonan |title=Structure presque quaternale sur une variété differentiable |journal=Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences |volume=261 |pages=5445–8 |year=1965 }}</ref> and Kraines<ref>{{cite journal |first=Vivian Yoh |last=Kraines |title=Topology of quaternionic manifolds |journal= Transactions of the American Mathematical Society |volume=122 |issue=2 |pages=357–367 |year=1966 
|doi=10.1090/S0002-9947-1966-0192513-X |jstor=1994553 |url=https://www.ams.org/tran/1966-122-02/S0002-9947-1966-0192513-X/S0002-9947-1966-0192513-X.pdf|doi-access=free }}</ref> who have independently proven that any such manifold admits a parallel 4-form <math>\Omega</math>. A quaternion-Kähler  analog of the hard Lefschetz theorem was
later proved<ref>{{cite journal|first=Edmond | last=Bonan|title=Sur l'algèbre extérieure d'une variété presque hermitienne quaternionique |journal= Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences|volume =295|year=1982|pages=115–118}}</ref> by Bonan.                                  
                                      
In the context of [[holonomy|Berger's classification of Riemannian holonomies]], quaternion-Kähler manifolds constitute the only class of irreducible, non-symmetric manifolds of special holonomy that are automatically [[Einstein manifold|Einstein]], but not automatically Ricci-flat. If the Einstein constant of a simply connected manifold with holonomy in <math>Sp(n) Sp(1)</math> is zero, where <math>n\geq 2</math>, then the holonomy is actually contained in <math>Sp(n)</math>, and the manifold is [[hyperkähler manifold|hyperkähler]]. This case is excluded from the definition by declaring quaternion-Kähler to mean not only that the holonomy group is contained in <math>Sp(n) Sp(1)</math>, but also that the manifold has non-zero (constant) scalar curvature.

With this convention, quaternion-Kähler manifolds can thus be naturally divided into those for which the [[Ricci curvature]] is positive, and those for which it is instead negative.

== Examples ==
There are no known examples of '''compact''' quaternion-Kähler manifolds that are not [[locally symmetric]]. (Again, [[hyperkähler]] manifolds are excluded from the discussion by fiat.) On the other hand, there are many [[Quaternion-Kähler symmetric space|symmetric quaternion-Kähler manifolds]]; these were first classified by [[Joseph A. Wolf]],<ref>{{cite journal |first=Joseph A. |last=Wolf |title=Complex homogeneous contact manifolds and quaternionic symmetric spaces |journal=J. Math. Mech. |volume=14 |issue= 6|pages=1033–47 |year=1965 |jstor=24901319 }}
</ref> 
and so are known as [[Wolf space]]s. For any simple Lie group ''G'', there is a unique Wolf space ''G''/''K'' obtained as a quotient of ''G'' by a subgroup <math> K = K_0 \cdot \operatorname{SU}(2)</math>, where 
<math>SU(2)</math> is the subgroup associated with the highest root of ''G'', and ''K''<sub>0</sub> is its [[centralizer]] in ''G''. The Wolf spaces with positive Ricci curvature are compact and simply connected.
For example, if 
<math> G= Sp(n+1)</math>, the corresponding Wolf space is the '''[[quaternionic projective space]]'''
<math>\mathbb{HP}_n</math> of (right) quaternionic lines through the origin in <math>\mathbb{H}^{n+1}</math>.

A conjecture often attributed to LeBrun and Salamon (see below) asserts that all complete quaternion-Kähler manifolds of positive scalar curvature are symmetric. By contrast, however, constructions of Galicki-Lawson <ref>{{cite journal |last1=Galicki |first1=K. |last2=Lawson |first2=H.B. Jr. |title=Quaternionic reduction and quaternionic orbifolds |journal=Math. Ann. |volume=282 |pages=1–21 |year=1988 |doi=10.1007/BF01457009 |s2cid=120748113 |url=http://www.galicki.com/math/papers/pdf/MathAnn88.pdf}}</ref> and of LeBrun<ref>{{cite journal |author-link=Claude LeBrun |first=Claude |last=LeBrun |title=On complete quaternionic-Kähler manifolds |journal=Duke Math. J. |volume=63 |issue=3 |pages=723–743 |year=1991 |doi=10.1215/S0012-7094-91-06331-3 |url=https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/~claude/duke1991.pdf}}</ref> show that complete, non-locally-symmetric quaternion-Kähler manifolds of '''negative''' scalar curvature exist in great profusion. The Galicki-Lawson construction just cited also gives rise to vast numbers of compact non-locally-symmetric '''orbifold''' examples with '''positive''' Einstein constant, and many of these in turn give rise<ref>{{cite book |first1=Charles |last1=Boyer |first2=Krzysztof |last2=Galicki |title=Sasakian Geometry |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ERYZAQAAIAAJ |date=2008 |publisher=Oxford University Press |series=Oxford Mathematical Monographs |isbn=978-0-19-856495-9 }}</ref> to compact, non-singular [[Sasakian manifold|3-Sasakian]] [[Einstein manifold]]s of dimension <math>4n+3</math>.

== Twistor spaces ==

Questions about quaternion-Kähler manifolds can be translated into the language of complex geometry using the methods of ''twistor theory''; this fact is encapsulated in a theorem discovered independently by Salamon and Bérard-Bergery, and inspired by earlier work of Penrose. Let <math>M</math> be a quaternion-Kähler manifold, and <math>H</math> be the sub-bundle of <math>End(TM)</math> arising from the holonomy action of <math>\mathfrak{sp}(1) \subset \mathfrak{sp}(n)\oplus \mathfrak{sp}(1)</math>. Then <math>H</math> contains an <math>S^2</math>-bundle <math>Z\to M</math> consisting of all <math>j\in H</math> that satisfy <math>j^2=-1</math>. The points of <math>Z</math> thus represent complex structures on tangent spaces of <math>M</math>. Using this, the total space <math>Z</math> can then be equipped with a tautological [[almost complex manifold|almost complex structure]]. 
Salamon<ref>{{cite journal |first=Simon |last=Salamon |title=Quaternionic Kähler manifolds |journal=Invent. Math. |volume=67 |pages=143–171 |year=1982 |doi=10.1007/BF01393378 |bibcode=1982InMat..67..143S |s2cid=118575943 }}</ref> (and, independently, Bérard-Bergery<ref>{{harvnb|Besse|1987}}</ref>) proved that this almost complex structure is integrable, thereby making <math>Z</math> into a [[complex manifold]].

When the Ricci curvature of ''M'' is positive, ''Z'' is a [[Fano variety|Fano manifold]], and so, in particular, 
is a smooth projective algebraic complex variety. Moreover, it admits a [[Kähler–Einstein metric]], and, more importantly, comes equipped with a holomorphic [[contact manifold|contact structure]], corresponding to the horizontal spaces of the Riemannian connection on ''H''. These facts were used by LeBrun and Salamon<ref>{{cite journal |last1=LeBrun |first1=Claude |last2=Salamon |first2=Simon |title=Strong rigidity of positive quaternion-Kähler manifolds |journal=Invent. Math. |volume=118 |pages=109–132 |year=1994 |doi=10.1007/BF01231528 |bibcode=1994InMat.118..109L |s2cid=121184428 }}</ref> to prove that, up to isometry and rescaling, there are only finitely many positive-scalar-curvature compact quaternion-Kähler manifolds in any given dimension. This same paper also shows that any such manifold is actually a symmetric space unless its second homology is a finite group with non-trivial 2-torsion. Related techniques had also been used previously by Poon and Salamon<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Poon |first1=Y.S. |last2=Salamon |first2=S.M. |title=Quaternionic Kähler 8-manifolds with positive scalar curvature |journal=J. Differential Geom. |volume=33 |issue=2 |pages=363–378 |year=1991 |doi=10.4310/jdg/1214446322 |doi-access=free }}</ref> to show that there are no non-symmetric examples at all in dimension 8.

In the converse direction, a result of LeBrun<ref>{{cite journal |first=Claude |last=LeBrun |title=Fano manifolds, contact structures, and quaternionic geometry |journal=Internat. J. Math. |volume=6 |issue= 3|pages=419–437 |year=1995 |doi=10.1142/S0129167X95000146 |arxiv=dg-ga/9409001 |s2cid=18361986 }}</ref> shows that any Fano manifold that admits both a Kähler–Einstein metric and a holomorphic contact structure is actually the [[twistor space]] of a quaternion-Kähler manifold of positive scalar curvature, which is moreover unique up to isometries and rescalings.
